# uronode

**Node front end that lets other stations reach services on your machine**

- **Version recorded:** 2.15
- **Categories:** `emcomm`, `packet`
- **Upstream:** <https://uronode.sourceforge.net/>
- **Install after:** `ax25-tools`
- **Needs from the kernel:** `ax25` — checked against the running kernel at plan time; see [kernel-ax25](../reference/kernel-ax25.md)

## What it does

Answers inbound connections -- over AX.25, NET/ROM, Rose or TCP -- and presents a command prompt from which the caller can connect onward to another station, read a bulletin, reach a BBS, or use whatever else you have configured. It is the switchboard a packet node presents to the world.

## Why you would want it

A node is what makes a station useful to other people rather than only to you. If your machine is well sited or well connected, running a node lets others reach places they could not reach directly, which is most of what a packet network is.

## Before it will work

A configured AX.25 stack, and `ax25d` set up to hand inbound connections to uronode. Your callsign appears in that configuration and in what callers see.

## How it installs

- apt: `uronode`

## Known problems

Needs the kernel AX.25 stack, which Linux 7.1 removed (merge 64edfa65, 2026-04-24); on a 7.1 or newer kernel -- Kali rolling and Pop!_OS 24.04 on 7.1.5, measured 2026-09-04 -- the plan refuses or defers this unit by name. See `ax25-tools` and `docs/reference/kernel-ax25.md`. A node is a service other people use, and running one is a commitment: an unreliable node is worse for a network than no node. It relays traffic on your callsign's authority, so what passes through it is your responsibility in most jurisdictions. Configuration is several files and getting the ax25d handoff right is the usual sticking point.
